Photograph: Patipat Janthong/Reuters With 40 dead and a disaster declared across all 50 city districts, experts warn extreme flooding will only worsen across south-east Asia By Oliver Holmes and Ajit Niranjan Fri 2 Oct 2026 22.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google B angkok is used to absorbing the sudden afternoon downpours that inundate the city during the rainy season. Even streets in many central high-rise districts can briefly turn into rivers, with rats and cockroaches racing out of sewers and taking temporary refuge on trees and buildings as the subterranean world is flushed out. But every city has a breaking point, and this year rain fell so fast and so hard that whole neighbourhoods of the Thai capital have been transformed, not into rivers, but stagnant lakes. In parts of the city, roughly 300mm of rain – the equivalent of half a year of average rainfall in London – fell in about two days. View image in fullscreen A person wades through flood water in Lat Krabang district, Bangkok. Photograph: Rungroj Yongrit/EPA About 40 people died in flood-related incidents, according to the government. A number of the deaths were from drowning and several from accidental electrocution. Thousands of people stayed in more than 230 shelters across the city, authorities said. Suleemas Kurangkul, a 73-year-old resident of a block of flats whose ground floor stairs are still under water, said last weekend’s rain was not the usual evening storm but was constant, “like all day, all night”. “The water just kept rising,” said Suleemas, whose flat is above the waterline on the second floor. By the time she and her neighbours received a mobile phone warning, it was too late, and the street-level water was waist-high. The 1970s Khlong Chan flat compound in north-east Bangkok where Suleemas lives has become a symbol of the disaster. Photos have been shared across Thailand of the flats rising out of the brownish water, with the rooftops of parked cars barely peeking above the surface, although the authorities had managed to drain away the worst of it by Thursday. Later in the week, during a brief respite in the rain, Suleemas said the water had receded somewhat. “People are so happy to see the sunshine,” she said. “Yet, the smell is getting stronger. So much debris and rubbish floating all over the place.” Built on a vast floodplain of the Chao Phraya River, Bangkok, a megacity of millions, relies on a network of muddy canals to drain water, as well as pumps and dikes. But concrete construction has destroyed much of the canal network, and the city is unable to cope. The government has declared a flood disaster across all 50 of the city’s districts. Some neighbourhoods have turned into dystopian scenes, with people using blow-up paddling pools or, in one case, a floating fridge, as boats to reach their homes. One man was arrested for riding a jetski along a main road. View image in fullscreen A resident uses a floating fridge as a boat. Photograph: Rungroj Yongrit/EPA “It’s a lesson,” said Chaleerat Chamrasporn, 55, a resident. “The kids are into doomsday-themed content, so now they can see what the ‘end of the world’ is actually like, or rather, that this is just the beginning.” Flooding has also disrupted Bangkok’s main Suvarnabhumi airport, with about half ⁠of Thai Airways’ workforce unable to report for work at one point this week, causing thousands of items of luggage ​to pile up and forcing flight ​cancellations. Many schools have closed, and with much of the capital in gridlock even people in less affected areas have been stuck at home. Thailand’s prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, told reporters that Bangkok’s metropolitan area was still at risk from flood waters flowing in from ​the north, and said a war room had ‌been set up to monitor ‌the situation. Thailand’s weather ⁠agency has forecast more ​heavy rain for next week. View image in fullscreen People stand on benches on the flooded pavement in Ramkhamhaeng in Bangkok. Photograph: Lillian Suwanrumpha/AFP/Getty Images It is part of a pattern that seems to be setting in this part of the world. South-east Asia has already seen a worsening of extreme floods, scientists say, a trend that is set to worsen as fossil fuel pollutants bake the planet further. Hot seas evaporate more water and warm air can hold more moisture, allowing downpours to crash down with far more force. “In central Thailand, I can see from my maps, we have already seen a small but significant trend towards extreme rainfall,” said Nikolaos Skliris, an ocean scientist at the University of Southampton who has studied heavy rain in the region. “In the long-term, all models show this will be amplified – more rainfall, and more extreme rainfall.” It is too early for scientists to attribute these particular rains to climate breakdown without doing a study. They were caused by a low-pressure system that moved from an unusually warm South China Sea over Cambodia and Vietnam before getting stuck above Bangkok, which was fairly cool, data from Copernicus Climate Pulse showed. The picture is complicated by the emergence of an abnormally strong El Niño, a cyclical weather pattern that brings record heat and more violent extremes around the world. Its presence typically leads to drier summer conditions in south-east Asia but recent research suggests it still exacerbates days with extreme rainfall. Naim Laeni, a consultant and part-time university lecturer who co-authored a study on Bangkok’s flood resilience , said authorities had underestimated the strength of the rains, which persisted for days. The city’s drainage canals can handle about 60mm of rain an hour, rising to 80mm in upgraded sections, but localised bursts exceeded this while leaving too little time between periods of stress. “The government did not communicate the seriousness,” said Laeni. “Usually in Bangkok we receive heavy rain for a few hours, not for days.” View image in fullscreen People wade through a flooded area during heavy rain in Bangkok. Photograph: Patipat Janthong/Reuters Neighbouring Myanmar has suffered from the same weather system, with flash floods and blocked roads complicating rescue efforts in the country. Rescuers were pulling bodies from a landslide that devastated the village of Ka Det Nge Htein in Myanmar’s south at the weekend. That disaster had already claimed nine lives, and eight more people are missing under the mud in another village, local officials said. Civil war across the country, and a junta that restricts the media, have made it hard to get information, and hampered aid organisations. Back in Bangkok, pumping stations have been operating at full capacity, but it could be days before the waters fully drain. At her apartment complex, Suleemas said she would stay where she was with her neighbours. “It’s hard, yes, very hard,” she said. “But together we are fighting and biting through it. When we get together to help one another like this, our spirit can keep us on our feet; we can get through it all together.” Agence France-Presse contributed to this report Explore more on these topics Extreme weather Thailand Asia Pacific Flooding El Niño southern oscillation Climate crisis features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3rr.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The US removed all its bombers from the UK's RAF Fairford base last month after a major incident in September that police described as "suspicious" By Jack Burgess Published 3 hours ago The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe. The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed. One man, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national, is accused of communicating with contacts in the UK from a prison in New York where he is awaiting trial on previous charges. The other two are accused of doing the same from Iran. Iran has strongly denied any involvement in the RAF Fairford incident, which came to light when suspicious vans were reported near the base. Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident. Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said. It accuses the trio of planning attacks in Europe that were carried out under the name of a purportedly new group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (The Islamic Movement of the People of the Right Hand - HAYI). "Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the UK," the DOJ statement said. It added that the attacks involved "arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual US-British citizen". Two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green, north London, in April. A suspect is due to stand trial next year. "This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the US," FBI Director Kash Patel said. He added that one of the three "allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence" from detention. Patel said the accused were involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Armed police officers were posted outside the RAF Fairford base following the incident in September A major incident was declared on 27 September near the UK's RAF Fairford base, in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire, after three suspicious vans were seen near the airbase. No explosive materials were found in the vans, but a quantity of petrol was seized. The DOJ said that in August, al-Hassani "allegedly directed and paid associates" in the UK to "conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford terrorist plot". On 22 August, al-Hassani paid one individual to "perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford's perimeter", the department said. In September, al-Hassani paid several people to help him prepare for the plot, the DOJ also alleged. According to its statement, this included "procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel". The suspects then gave the vans an appearance of being used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business, the DOJ stated. "On 26 September, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base." The DOJ also said al-Hassani was "in frequent communication" with the van drivers and helped to direct them where to drive. "At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route," it added. It was in the very early hours of 27 September, that the vans were spotted by a local farmer who was heading home from a party, and called the police. What we know about RAF Fairford counter-terror probe Published 1 October The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident. Two British nationals appeared in court last month in connection with the alleged Iran-linked plot. The US withdrew all its bombers from RAF Fairford after the incident, with President Donald Trump citing "some threats" to the base as the reason. RAF Fairford has been used by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades. In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from there to the Middle East for "defensive" strikes on Iran. In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
